analysis.one_liner: Bars USDA from buying meat or processed food made by workers paid below local prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would require federal meat and food suppliers to pay at least the local prevailing wage, was introduced in July 2023 and never received a committee vote or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop the Department of Agriculture from buying meat, poultry, or processed food from any U.S. plant whose workers are paid below the prevailing local wage and benefits rate, as determined by the Department of Labor using local collective bargaining agreements as a benchmark. The idea is to use the government's purchasing power to lift pay in low-wage meatpacking and food-processing jobs. It would not cut any worker's negotiated union contract. It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at meatpacking, poultry, and food-processing plants that sell to the federal government. Any plant paying below the local prevailing rate would have to raise wages and benefits to keep its USDA contracts. Workers covered by union contracts are explicitly protected from any reduction, and unions gain because their local contracts become the benchmark for pay.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits USDA from purchasing meat, poultry, or processed food produced by U.S. workers paid below the prevailing local rate for wages and fringe benefits [S2][S3].
Requires the Department of Labor to set those prevailing rates and to take existing local collective bargaining agreements into account, so union standards become the measuring stick [S2][S3].
Bars a prevailing-rate requirement from reducing any worker's wages or benefits already agreed to in a collective bargaining contract [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meatpackers, poultry processors, and food manufacturers that supply the federal government at below-prevailing wages would face higher labor costs on the portion of production tied to USDA purchases. Federal food purchases — for school meals, military feeding, and food assistance — could cost somewhat more if suppliers pass the higher wages through.

drawbacks.text: It is a narrow lever: it only affects the slice of meat and processed food that USDA buys for federal programs, so most meatpacking workers in plants without federal contracts would see no benefit [S2][S3].

Higher supplier labor costs would likely be passed through to the government, raising the cost of federal food programs such as school meals and military food service — a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S3].

Compliance and prevailing-wage determinations add administrative requirements that could burden smaller processors more than large firms with compliance staff, potentially tilting contracting toward bigger companies [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a genuine problem — meatpacking and poultry processing are among the lowest-paid, most dangerous industrial jobs — but through a deliberately narrow channel: only workers on USDA's supply chain. The wage gains would be real for that group; the costs are modestly higher federal food procurement prices and some compliance burden. It was a targeted, low-cost pilot of prevailing-wage rules rather than an industry-wide wage mandate, and it never got far enough for those tradeoffs to be tested or debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its livestock subcommittee, where it sat with no markup, no vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the Food Worker Pay Standards Act on July 11, 2023, joined by Rep. Greg Casar [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the day it was introduced [S5].
On August 24, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry — the last action of any kind on the bill [S5].
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meatpackers, poultry processors, and food manufacturers that supply USDA at below-prevailing wages kept their contracts and their labor costs unchanged. No federal food program faced any price increase. Workers at those plants gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Mark Pocan
for.role: Sponsor, House sponsor of the Food Worker Pay Standards Act
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Agriculture Committee

for.name: Rep. Greg Casar
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Glenn Thompson, R-PA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction, sent it to the Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry Subcommittee, and took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report — for the remaining year and a half of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no positional record exists; both sponsors were Democrats, no Republican cosponsored it, and a Republican-led committee took no action.

industries.note: Suppliers paying below local prevailing rates would have to raise pay on USDA-bound production, cutting into the low-wage labor model. For the workers at those plants, higher pay runs alongside the public's interest in decent jobs; the added cost flows partly to federal food programs. The bill died, so nothing changed.

The bill covers processed food as defined in federal food law, so food processors selling to USDA faced the same prevailing-wage condition. Like meatpackers, they keep their existing arrangements because the bill never advanced.

Contractors would face new wage-compliance requirements and possibly higher costs passed through from suppliers, and prevailing-rate paperwork tends to favor larger firms with compliance staff. They had a direct financial interest in the bill not moving.
